lessons.title: What is AI, and why is it in your office?
lessons.objective: After this lesson, you’ll be able to say in plain language what AI is, why it applies to research administration, and what this course will do for you.
lessons.content:
Before any tools or terminology, the big picture.

**What AI is** — software that has learned patterns from enormous amounts of example text, well enough to do useful reading and writing tasks on new material. That’s it. Not a mind, not magic — a very capable pattern machine.

**Why it’s suddenly everywhere** — in the last few years these systems got good enough at ordinary language that they can do real office work: read a 50-page proposal and pull out the PI, the budget, the dates; summarize a progress report; draft a routine email.

**Why it matters for research administration** — your job is unusually document-heavy. Proposals, award notices, subawards, progress reports — most of the work is reading documents and moving what they say into spreadsheets, systems, and summaries. That’s exactly the work this technology is best at drafting for you. It will not make judgment calls, know your institution’s policies, or take responsibility — that stays yours.

**How this course helps** — module by module, you’ll turn one real process at a time into an AI-assisted pipeline you control and verify. The course is self-paced and saves your reading place. Reading, source checks, repairs and assessed work take different amounts of time; no fixed module-completion time has been measured. Start with the course training examples and available supported tools.

lessons.title: Structured vs. unstructured data
lessons.objective: After this lesson, you’ll be able to tell structured from unstructured data and explain why converting one to the other is the heart of this course.
lessons.content:
One distinction carries this whole course — and it has nothing to do with how AI works under the hood.

**Unstructured data** is prose meant for people: a proposal PDF, an award letter, a progress report. The information is in there, but every document says it differently and puts it somewhere different.

**Structured data** is information in labeled slots: your award-tracking spreadsheet, a sponsor form, a database record. Every row has the same columns — PI, sponsor, amount, dates — so you can sort it, total it, compare it, report on it.

Now name a large part of research administration work: reading unstructured documents and re-typing what they say into structured form. Proposal arrives → fields go into the tracking sheet. Award letter arrives → terms go into the system.

That conversion — unstructured in, structured out — is precisely what Vandalizer automates. You define the columns once; it drafts the row for every document. You review instead of re-type. When later modules say “extraction,” this is all they mean.

lessons.title: What is an LLM, really?
lessons.objective: After this lesson, you'll be able to explain why LLMs make mistakes and why they're still useful.
lessons.content:
A Large Language Model (LLM) is not thinking. It is not sentient. It does not understand your documents the way you do.

An LLM is a sophisticated pattern-completion engine trained on vast amounts of text. When you give it a prompt, it predicts the most likely next words based on patterns it learned during training. This is both why it's capable and why it makes mistakes.

It's capable because human language follows patterns. A grant proposal has a predictable structure: PI name, institution, budget, aims. The LLM has seen thousands of similar documents and can reliably identify these patterns.

It makes mistakes because pattern-matching is not understanding. The LLM doesn't know what a budget is. It knows that numbers near the word "budget" are likely dollar amounts. When the pattern breaks (unusual formatting, ambiguous language), the LLM may confidently produce wrong answers.

options.text: Thinking through the problem logically, like a human would
options.explanation: LLMs don't "think". They predict patterns based on training data.

options.text: Predicting the most likely next words based on patterns from training data
options.explanation: Correct! LLMs are pattern-completion engines trained on vast text.

options.text: Looking up answers in a database of facts
options.explanation: LLMs don't have a database; they learned patterns from training text.

options.text: Running a search engine to find relevant information
options.explanation: LLMs generate text from learned patterns, not from searching the internet.

lessons.title: What AI is genuinely good at
lessons.objective: After this lesson, you'll know which research admin tasks are best suited for AI automation.
lessons.content:
AI excels at tasks that involve pattern recognition across large volumes of text:

• **Extracting specific information** from long documents — Finding the PI name, budget, and project period in a 50-page proposal.
• **Summarizing** — Condensing a progress report into key findings and milestones.
• **Comparing across documents** — Identifying differences between two versions of a budget justification.
• **Drafting routine text** — Generating first drafts of compliance summaries or progress report templates.
• **Processing many documents consistently** — Applying the same extraction to 200 proposals and getting results in the same format every time.

The common thread: these are tasks where a human would be doing repetitive reading and data entry. AI handles the volume; you handle the judgment.

lessons.title: What AI is genuinely bad at
lessons.objective: After this lesson, you'll be able to identify AI limitations and avoid common pitfalls in research administration.
lessons.content:
Honesty about AI's limitations is essential for responsible use in research administration:

• **Judgment calls requiring institutional knowledge** — AI doesn't know your university's internal policies, political dynamics, risk tolerance, or historical context.
• **Catching its own mistakes** — An LLM cannot reliably self-check. If it extracts the wrong budget figure, it won't flag the error. That's your job.
• **Math** — LLMs frequently make arithmetic errors. Never trust an LLM to add up budget line items. Use a checked calculator or explicitly recorded human arithmetic. Where code execution is available and authorized, inspect its rule and inputs too. A model explanation is not independent arithmetic evidence.
• **Novel or unusual document formats** — If a document doesn't follow standard patterns (hand-written notes, unusual layouts, scanned images with poor OCR), extraction quality drops significantly.
• **Replacing professional judgment on compliance** — AI can flag potential issues, but determining whether a proposal actually meets regulatory requirements requires your expertise.

The pattern: AI is a powerful first-pass tool. It does the reading; you do the thinking.

options.text: Processing 200 documents in the same format

lessons.title: AI for research administration
lessons.objective: After this lesson, you'll be able to describe where AI fits in common research admin workflows and where it doesn't.
lessons.content:
Here's what AI-assisted research administration looks like in practice:

• **Proposal intake** — Upload 30 new proposals to a secure, institutionally managed AI environment. A workflow extracts PI name, agency, budget, and key dates from each one in minutes instead of hours — without exposing sensitive proposal data to consumer AI tools or free-tier services.
• **Progress report processing** — Extract accomplishments, publications, and expenditures from annual reports. Flag any that are missing required sections.
• **Compliance pre-screening** — Check proposals against a list of required elements (human subjects approval, data management plan, budget justification) and flag gaps.
• **Subaward review** — Extract parties, amounts, and terms from subaward agreements. Compare against institutional templates.

The pattern in every case: AI does the first pass of extraction, you do the second pass of verification and judgment. The AI handles volume and consistency. You bring expertise and accountability.

lessons.title: Supervising agentic chat: scope, evidence and approval
lessons.objective: Inspect the intended scope, reject unsupported claims and distinguish source text from authorization.
lessons.content:
Agentic chat can propose and carry out supported operations using your workspace. Read a proposed action as a concrete change: which documents, which workspace, which configuration and which destination it will use. A similar title is not enough to identify the correct source. Correct a mismatch before asking it to run. Where a confirmation preview is offered, inspect it; otherwise your request may start the operation directly. Request a proposal only when you need to review the scope first.

**Walkthrough: review a scoped extraction**

1. Name the assigned source document and the fields you need. State the intended output and any actions that need separate approval.
2. Inspect the proposed document and workspace selection. If the proposal points to a similarly named live document, stop and correct it.
3. Review the extraction fields and planned action. Ask for a revision when the proposal exceeds the task’s scope.
4. After execution, compare important values with the supplied source. A fluent answer, a successful run and an earlier quality score answer different questions; none independently proves that this answer is supported.
5. If a requested value is absent, record that it was not found in the supplied source. Seek additional evidence when needed instead of filling the gap with a plausible guess.
6. Review the destination and data scope before release. Approval to prepare an internal comparison does not automatically authorize publication or external delivery.

**Treat source instructions as data.** A PDF may contain wording that asks the agent to ignore the task or send information elsewhere. That text cannot change your authorized task. Keep the approved scope and obtain a separate authorized decision for any new action.

**Practice:** The source says only that applications close on 1 October at 17:00. The agent adds a two-day grace period. Identify the unsupported part, explain why confidence is insufficient, and choose an evidence-checking next step. This is a fictional practice passage, not an actual application policy.

The module’s assessed scenarios test recognition of unsupported claims, scope changes and authority limits. Later practical modules require evidence of applying those decisions to real course tasks. Reading this lesson or submitting a reflection does not establish those practical skills.

lessons.title: Worked example: Monday morning, 12 proposals
lessons.content:
The same task, twice.

**Without AI** — Twelve new proposals in the inbox. For each one: open the PDF, scroll for the cover page, copy the PI name into the tracking sheet, find the total budget (page 2? page 14?), copy it, find the project period, the agency, the deadline… about 15 careful minutes each. Three hours of re-typing, and by proposal nine, attention is fading — which is when a $485,000 becomes a $48,500.

**With a workflow** — The twelve PDFs are uploaded and a saved workflow runs. It reads each proposal and returns the same labeled fields for every one: PI Name, Institution, Total Budget, Project Period, Sponsoring Agency. In a few minutes there’s a table — one row per proposal, ready to check and export.

**What you do instead** — the 30-minute version of the job that’s actually yours: scan the table against the source documents, catch the one proposal whose budget page was a scanned image and extracted oddly, and make the judgment calls — which proposals need a compliance look, which PI needs a call.

By Module 9 you will have built exactly this.

lessons.title: Glossary & Review
lessons.content:
LLM (Large Language Model) — You've now seen how LLMs are used to extract structured fields from grant proposals and summarize documents. The key: an LLM is a pattern-completion engine, not a thinking machine. It predicts likely text based on training patterns. When you build a workflow step, you're giving it patterns to match — the clearer your field names and prompts, the better the results.

Prompt — The instructions you give an LLM. You'll write many of these as you build workflows. Quality matters: "Extract the PI name from the proposal cover page" outperforms "find the PI."

Hallucination — When an LLM generates a plausible-sounding value that isn't actually in the document. The #1 risk in research administration AI use. It's why you'll learn to build validation plans in Module 8.

Structured Output — The mechanism that makes batch processing possible. Instead of free-form text, the LLM is constrained to return JSON matching your field definitions — same fields, same format, every document, every time.

JSON — The fill-in-the-form format structured output arrives in: each of your field names paired with the value found for it, like a completed intake form. You will see JSON in results; you never have to write it.

Token — The unit AI models use to measure text — roughly ¾ of a word. The only time it matters to you: very long documents can exceed what a model reads at once, the way an email attachment can exceed a size limit.

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) — How the chat feature works. Relevant document excerpts are retrieved and provided to the LLM before it answers. This grounds responses in your actual documents rather than the LLM's training data.

lessons.title: What is a workflow?
lessons.objective: After this lesson, you'll understand how workflows differ from ad-hoc chat and why that matters for research administration.
lessons.content: A workflow is a reusable pipeline that processes a document through a series of defined steps — build it once, run it against any document. Unlike ad-hoc chat, workflows produce consistent, structured output. That consistency is what lets you process 500 grant proposals the same way you process one.

lessons.title: What you'll build
lessons.content:
Here's the end state for this module's lab exercise:

• A workflow called something like "Grant Proposal Extractor"
• An Extraction with at least 5 fields: PI Name, Total Budget, Sponsoring Agency, Project Period, Institution
• A run result showing Dr. Sarah Chen extracted from the sample NSF proposal, with a budget of $485,000

The lessons that follow explain each piece. By the time you reach the lab, every step will be familiar.

lessons.title: The document pipeline
lessons.objective: After this lesson, you'll understand what happens to a document between upload and extraction.
lessons.content:
When you upload a document, Vandalizer prepares it for you automatically — you never manage any of this:

1. **It reads the text out of the file** — PDFs, Word documents, spreadsheets, web pages.
2. **It builds an index of the content** — like the index at the back of a book, so questions and searches can jump straight to the right passage.

That’s all you need to know to use it. When a workflow runs an Extraction step, the AI reads the document text alongside your field list and hands back one filled-in record — every field name paired with the value it found.

*For the curious (safe to skip):* the index is built by splitting the text into overlapping passages and storing them in a search database — the technique behind the chat feature’s ability to quote your documents.

lessons.title: Build your first workflow
lessons.objective: After this lesson, you'll be ready to run your first extraction workflow on a real document.
lessons.content:
When you start the lab exercise, here's what you'll do:

1. Click **Set Up Lab** (the button at the top of this module) to load the sample NSF proposal into your workspace.
2. Go to the **Library** tab and click **New** to create a new workflow.
3. Give your workflow a clear name, like "Grant Proposal Extractor", and add a description such as "Extracts key details from grant proposals".
4. Add a step and give it a name, like "Extract Grant Details". Then add an Extraction task to that step.
5. In the Extraction task settings, select an existing Extraction or create a new one.
6. Add at least 3 fields to your Extraction — for example: "Principal Investigator", "Funding Amount", "Sponsoring Agency".
7. Select the sample NSF proposal in the file browser — tick the checkbox next to its name (opening the file in the viewer also selects it). **The Run button stays greyed out until a document is selected**; its tooltip says what’s missing.
8. Click **Run** and review the extracted results in the output panel.

lessons.title: Why structured extraction matters
lessons.content: Unstructured AI responses vary every time — different formatting, different phrasing, different levels of detail. Structured extraction forces the AI to return consistent, machine-readable JSON. This means you can reliably extract the same fields from hundreds of documents and compare, aggregate, or export the results. It turns documents from unstructured text into queryable data.

lessons.title: Glossary & Review
lessons.content:
Workflow — You just built one. A saved pipeline that processes documents through a series of steps. The recipe analogy holds: define it once, run it against any document. The extraction workflow from this module is the foundation for everything that follows.

Step — One stage in your pipeline. Your first workflow had one step (extraction). Later modules add reasoning and delivery steps to create more powerful pipelines.

Task — The specific operation inside a step. The Extraction task you configured defined which fields the AI should find and return as one filled-in record (JSON — the form-like format from Module 0; you read it, never write it).

Extraction — The collection of fields you defined. Think of it as your data dictionary — it tells the LLM exactly what to look for and what format to return it in.

Extract Key — Each individual field in your Extraction: "PI Name", "Total Budget", "Sponsoring Agency". Well-named extract keys get better results because the LLM uses the name as a clue about what to find.

title: Thinking in Workflows
subtitle: See Your Work as Automatable Processes
description: Before you can build a workflow, you need to see your work differently. This module teaches you to recognize the repeatable processes hiding in your daily tasks, identify which parts are suitable for AI, and which parts need your expertise.
objectives: Recognize repeatable processes in your research administration work
Identify which parts of a process are AI-suitable vs. human-judgment
Apply the process decomposition framework to a real task from your work
tips: Think about the tasks you do every week that follow the same pattern
The best workflow candidates are tasks where you spend most of your time reading and re-typing
Don't try to automate everything — the goal is to automate the tedious parts so you can focus on the important parts

lessons.title: From one workflow to many
lessons.objective: After this lesson, you'll be able to identify repeatable processes in your daily work that are ready for automation.
lessons.content:
You've built a basic workflow. Now the question is: what else in your office should be a workflow?

Module 1 taught you the mechanics. This module gives you a framework for finding the processes worth automating. The pattern you're looking for: any task where you spend 80% of your time reading documents and 20% making decisions about what you found. The reading is automatable. The deciding stays yours.

By the end of this module, you'll have mapped a real process from your own work to a workflow architecture — not a hypothetical, but something you could actually build next.

lessons.title: Finding the repetition
lessons.objective: After this lesson, you'll have a practical test for identifying which processes to automate.
lessons.content:
The best candidates for workflows are tasks that share three properties:

1. **You do them repeatedly** — not once, but dozens or hundreds of times. Processing proposals, reviewing progress reports, checking compliance documents.

2. **You follow the same steps each time** — you look for the same information, in the same kinds of documents, and produce the same kind of output.

3. **Most of the time is spent reading, not thinking** — you spend 80% of your time finding information in documents and 20% making decisions about it.

Here's a quick test: could you write step-by-step instructions for a new hire to do this task? If yes, it's a workflow. If the instructions would be "use your judgment," that specific step stays human.

Common research admin processes that pass this test:
• Processing incoming proposals (extracting key fields)
• Reviewing progress reports (checking completeness)
• Pre-screening for compliance (finding required elements)
• Summarizing subaward terms (extracting parties and obligations)
• Preparing data for reports (gathering numbers from multiple documents)

knowledgeCheck.question: What makes a process a good candidate for AI automation?

options.text: It requires deep institutional knowledge and professional judgment
options.explanation: Tasks requiring judgment should stay with humans — AI handles the repetitive reading part.

options.text: It's repetitive, document-based, and most time is spent reading rather than thinking
options.explanation: Correct! The best AI candidates are repetitive tasks where you spend most time extracting information from documents.

options.text: It only happens once or twice a year
options.explanation: Rare tasks don't benefit much from automation — the setup cost outweighs the time saved.

options.text: It involves making complex financial decisions
options.explanation: Complex decisions require human expertise. AI is better at the extraction that feeds into those decisions.

lessons.title: The AI suitability test
lessons.objective: After this lesson, you'll have a decision framework for choosing between Extraction, Code Execution, and keeping a step human.
lessons.content:
Not every step in your process should be automated. Here's a practical framework:

**AI-suitable** (automate these):
• Reading a document and finding specific, fixed fields → Extraction
• Reading a short or context-heavy document and answering a question about it → Prompt, given the whole document
• Summarizing or paraphrasing document content → Prompt
• Comparing information across documents → Prompt
• Reformatting data from one structure to another → Formatter
• Drafting routine text based on extracted data → Prompt

**Use code, not AI**:
• Adding up numbers or computing percentages → Code Execution
• Date calculations or comparisons → Code Execution
• Applying deterministic rules ("if budget > $500K, flag for review") → Code Execution

**Keep human**:
• Deciding whether something meets a policy requirement
• Interpreting ambiguous or unusual situations
• Making recommendations that require institutional context
• Anything where a mistake has serious consequences and can't be easily caught

The pattern: AI reads and extracts. Code computes. Humans judge.

lessons.title: Walkthrough: Mapping a real process
lessons.content:
Let's decompose "processing incoming proposals" step by step:

1. **Receive the proposal document** (PDF) → Input: this is your workflow trigger.

2. **Find PI name, institution, budget, project dates, agency** → AI-suitable: this is reading and extracting. Map to an Extraction step.

3. **Check whether required sections are present** (data management plan, budget justification, biosketches) → AI-suitable: checking for presence of sections. Map to a Prompt step.

4. **Verify the budget adds up** → Use code: map to a Code Execution step that sums extracted line items.

5. **Decide whether to flag for compliance review** → Keep human: this requires institutional judgment. This is where your workflow ends and your review begins.

6. **Enter data into your tracking system** → The workflow's structured output makes this copy-paste or even automated via API.

Result: a 3-step workflow (Extract → Check sections → Verify budget) that does 70% of the work, leaving you to do the 30% that requires your expertise.

lessons.title: Common processes that become workflows
lessons.content:
Here are the most common research administration processes and how they map to workflows:

• **Proposal intake** — Extract key fields, check completeness, flag gaps. 3-4 steps.
• **Progress report review** — Extract accomplishments, publications, expenditures. Summarize and compare to milestones. 3 steps.
• **Compliance pre-screening** — Extract required elements, check against a compliance checklist, produce a gap report. 3-4 steps.
• **Budget review** — Extract line items, compute totals, compare to limits, produce a summary. 4 steps.
• **Subaward processing** — Extract parties, amounts, terms, deliverables. Flag deviations from templates. 3 steps.
• **Award closeout** — Gather final expenditures, publications, and deliverables from multiple documents. 4-5 steps.

Notice the pattern: every workflow starts by *reading* the document and ends with either a human review point or a produced deliverable. The middle steps are where analysis, comparison, and computation happen.

The reading step is usually an Extraction, because these processes want the same fixed fields from every document. It does not have to be. A two-page award amendment or a sponsor email is often better read by a Prompt that sees the whole file — there are no fields to pull, and the answer depends on the full context. Extraction is a tool for a job, not a mandatory first step.

lessons.title: Worked example: mapping progress-report review
lessons.content:
Apply the five elements to a second real process, end to end.

**Input** — A PI’s annual progress report (PDF) lands two weeks before the sponsor deadline.

**Steps** — (1) Read it and pull out accomplishments, publications, students supported, and expenditures to date. (2) Check that every section the sponsor requires is present. (3) Compare reported spending against the award budget. (4) Draft the cover summary for the sponsor portal.

**Decision points** — Is the spending variance large enough to question? Is a thin “Results” section acceptable this year? These stay human.

**Handoffs** — Missing sections go back to the PI; a large variance goes to the fiscal officer.

**Output** — A completed portal entry and a filed summary.

Now the sort: steps 1 and 2 are reading → AI-suitable (Extraction, Prompt). Step 3 is arithmetic → code, never an LLM. Step 4 is drafting from extracted data → AI-suitable, human-reviewed. The decision points and handoffs stay exactly where they are — with you.

lessons.title: Glossary & Review
lessons.content:
Use these five elements to describe any process you're considering automating. You've seen them applied to proposal intake — now practice applying them to a process from your own work.

Input — What triggers this process? Usually a document arriving: a proposal, a report, a subaward agreement, a budget justification.

Steps — The discrete actions you take, in order. Each step has a clear purpose: "find the PI name," "check the budget," "write a summary."

Decision Points — Where you apply judgment: "Is this budget reasonable?" "Does this meet compliance requirements?" These are where human expertise is essential and AI steps back.

Handoffs — Where work passes between people: "Send to compliance officer for review," "Return to PI for corrections."

Output — What's produced at the end: a completed form, a summary report, a recommendation, data entered into a system.

title: Workflow Design
subtitle: From Process Map to Pipeline Architecture
description: Now that you can decompose a process, learn how to translate it into a specific workflow architecture. Which task types fit which steps? How should data flow? Where do humans stay in the loop?
objectives: Map process steps to specific Vandalizer task types
Understand the extract-reason-deliver pattern — and when Extraction is the wrong first step
Design workflows that support human review, not replace it

lessons.title: From process map to workflow architecture
lessons.objective: After this lesson, you'll be able to map each step in a process to a specific Vandalizer task type.
lessons.content:
In Module 2, you decomposed a process into steps and identified which are AI-suitable vs. which stay human. Now you'll map each AI-suitable step to a specific Vandalizer task type — turning your process map into a buildable architecture.

The mapping is straightforward:
• "Find specific fields in a document" → Extraction task with an Extraction
• "Read a short or context-heavy document and answer a question about it" → Prompt task with the document as its input (no Extraction first)
• "Analyze or summarize the extracted data" → Prompt task
• "Compute, total, or apply rules" → A permitted deterministic calculation with checked inputs, such as a calculator or authorized Code Execution task. Record an external calculation explicitly before a later model step relies on it
• "Check a document for specific sections or elements" → Prompt task
• "Produce a formatted report or export" → Document Renderer or Data Export
• "Compare this document to another" → Add Document + Prompt task

The key insight: you're not starting from scratch asking "what can this tool do?" You're starting from your process and asking "which tool handles this step?"

lessons.title: The extract-reason-deliver pattern
lessons.objective: After this lesson, you'll understand the most reliable workflow pattern for research administration and why it works.
lessons.content:
The most common and most effective workflow pattern in research administration has three phases:

1. **Extract** — Pull structured data from the document. This is your Extraction step with a well-designed Extraction. The output is clean, consistent JSON.

2. **Reason** — Analyze the extracted data. This might be a Prompt step that summarizes findings, a Code Execution step that computes totals, or both. The output is analysis or computed results.

3. **Deliver** — Produce something useful. A formatted report, a CSV export, a compliance checklist, or structured data ready for your tracking system.

This pattern works because it separates concerns. If your final report is wrong, you can check: did the extraction get the right data? (Check step 1's output.) Did the analysis interpret it correctly? (Check step 2.) You can fix the broken step without rebuilding the whole workflow.

**The Extract phase is optional, and task-dependent.** "Extract" means *get what you need out of the document*, and the Extraction task is one way to do that — the right way when you want the same fixed fields from every document, when the document is long enough that the reasoning step should not see all of it, or when you need values you can check one by one. For a short or context-heavy document — a two-page amendment letter, a sponsor email, a memo where the answer depends on the whole narrative — an Extraction step in front adds a hop without adding reliability. Send the whole file to the Prompt instead: the first step after the Document trigger receives the workflow's documents automatically, and any later step can choose **Workflow Documents** or **Selected Document** as its input source. Teams that have tried both report that for those documents the direct Prompt gives better answers. Reason and Deliver stay the same either way.

knowledgeCheck.question: When is it better to skip the Extraction step and send the whole document straight to a Prompt?

options.text: Never — a workflow should always start with an Extraction task
options.explanation: Extraction is optional and task-dependent. It earns its place when you need fixed fields or checkable values; a short or context-heavy document is often read better by a Prompt that sees the whole file.

options.text: When the document is short or the answer depends on its full context, and you don't need fixed fields
options.explanation: Correct! A two-page letter or a memo has no field list to pull and its meaning lives in the whole text. The first step after the Document trigger receives the document automatically — no Extraction needed. Reason and Deliver still follow.

options.text: When the document is very long
options.explanation: Long documents are where Extraction earns its keep: it narrows what the reasoning step sees and gives you values you can verify one by one.

options.text: When you need machine-readable output for a spreadsheet
options.explanation: Consistent, structured fields are exactly what the Extraction task is for. That is the case where you keep it.

lessons.title: Designing for your reviewer
lessons.objective: After this lesson, you'll be able to design workflow output that makes human review fast rather than cumbersome.
lessons.content:
Here's a truth about AI in research administration: someone will always review the output. Maybe it's you, maybe it's a compliance officer, maybe it's a PI. Your workflow should make that review easy and efficient.

Design principles for reviewable output:

• **Show your sources** — When the workflow extracts a budget figure, the output should make it easy to verify against the source document.
• **Flag uncertainty** — If a field couldn't be found or the value seems unusual, the output should say so.
• **Structure for scanning** — Make the source values, unresolved issues and required decisions easy to find. Scanning helps locate review work; it does not establish that every value is correct.
• **Separate data from analysis** — Show the raw extracted data first, then the analysis or recommendations.

The workflow's job is not to eliminate review. It's to make review fast and focused.

lessons.title: Walkthrough: Designing a compliance review pipeline
lessons.content:
Process: "Check whether a grant proposal includes all required compliance elements."

**Step 1** — Decompose the process:
• Read the proposal and identify which compliance sections are present
• Extract specific compliance data (human subjects, data management, conflict of interest)
• Compare against the required elements checklist
• Produce a gap report showing what's present and what's missing

**Step 2** — Map to task types:
• "Read and extract compliance data" → Extraction task
• "Compare against checklist" → Prompt task
• "Produce gap report" → Document Renderer task

**Step 3** — Design data flow:
• Step 1 output: JSON with compliance field values (or "not found")
• Step 2 input: that JSON. Output: analysis text with present/missing/incomplete categories
• Step 3 input: analysis text. Output: formatted compliance checklist document

Result: A 3-step workflow. Upload a proposal, click Run, download a compliance checklist.

lessons.title: When to split, when to combine
lessons.content:
A common question: should this be one step or two?

**Split into separate steps when:**
• You'd want to check the intermediate output
• The operations are different types — extraction and analysis are different skills
• You might reuse one part
• Debugging would be easier

**Combine into one step when:**
• The operations are tightly coupled
• The intermediate output isn't useful on its own
• The combined prompt is simple and focused
• The document is short or context-heavy and one focused Prompt over the whole file answers the question — an Extraction in front would only add a hop

Rule of thumb: start with more steps. You can always combine later once you know the workflow works. But splitting a monolithic step that's producing bad output is much harder than combining two steps that work well individually.

lessons.title: Worked example: designing subaward intake
lessons.content:
Process: “A signed subaward agreement arrives; get its terms into our tracking system and flag anything unusual.”

**Decompose** — (1) Pull the parties, amounts, period, deliverables, and reporting requirements out of the agreement. (2) Compare those terms against our standard template. (3) Write up deviations for the subaward officer. (4) Enter the data.

**Map to task types** — (1) Extraction task — structured fields. (2) Prompt task — “compare these extracted terms to the standard terms below; list deviations.” (3) Document Renderer — a one-page deviation memo. (4) The workflow’s structured output makes entry copy-paste.

**Design the data flow** — Step 1 outputs labeled fields; step 2 receives them (not the whole 40-page agreement — cleaner input, better analysis); step 3 formats step 2’s findings. A 40-page agreement with fixed terms is exactly where Extraction belongs. If the input were a two-page amendment letter instead, step 1 would be a Prompt reading the letter itself, and the pipeline would be two steps.

**Reviewer check** — the memo leads with the extracted terms table, then the flagged deviations, so the officer verifies in one glance. Three steps, one human checkpoint at the end — built in Module 5.

lessons.title: Chat-driven workflow design (v5.0)
lessons.objective: After this lesson, you'll be able to design and dispatch workflows from conversation, using the agent as a design partner.
lessons.content:
In Vandalizer 5.0, you don't have to translate your process map into a workflow by yourself. The agent can help.

**Design in chat.** Describe the process in plain English: *"I need a 3-step workflow for subaward review. Step 1 extracts parties, amounts, and compliance terms. Step 2 analyzes key obligations. Step 3 formats a compliance summary."* The agent proposes an architecture. Check whether each task type fits its input and purpose, then inspect and refine the saved configuration in the editor.

**Dispatch from chat.** Once built, you don't navigate to the workflow every time — you just ask: *"Run the subaward review on this agreement."* Check the named workflow and intended input before confirming the run. Inspect its actual status and results. A configured Approval step can pause for review before later work; inspect the reviewer, placement and timeout settings rather than assuming every run has that boundary.

**Build faster with propose-then-refine.** For extractions specifically, you can say *"Propose an extraction set for NIH R01 proposals based on this document"* and the agent analyzes the document, suggests fields, and creates the template on confirmation. Review the proposed fields and inspect the saved settings; no fixed time saving is established.

The trade-off is still the same as any AI output: the agent's proposal is a starting point, not the final design. Use it to skip boilerplate, then apply your expertise to the parts that matter.

lessons.title: Glossary & Review
lessons.content:
These are the design decisions you'll face for every workflow you build. You've seen them applied in the compliance review walkthrough — use this as a reference when designing your own pipelines.

Step granularity — How many steps should your workflow have? Each step should do one clear thing. If you can't describe a step's purpose in one sentence, split it.

Task type selection — Choose the simplest task type that gets the job done. If you need structured data from a document, use Extraction — don't write a Prompt asking the LLM to produce JSON. If you need a judgement or a narrative about a short document, a Prompt reading the document itself is usually the simpler tool. Extraction is a choice, not a mandatory first step.

Data flow — Inspect the saved input source for each step and any task override. Step Input uses the previous output; Workflow Documents supplies the run's documents; a Selected Document supplies that configured source. Later steps do not automatically receive all original context. Keep required references available to the operation that needs them.

Human checkpoints — Place the required review before the action whose consequences depend on it. Reviewing a final internal draft may be appropriate; reviewing after a send cannot prevent that send. Configure and test a supported pause or keep the later action separate. A written request for approval is not itself a runtime gate.

Error tolerance — What happens if the LLM extracts a field incorrectly? Design your workflow so errors are visible in the output, not hidden. Show source data alongside conclusions.

title: Extraction Engine
subtitle: Master the Extraction Pipeline
description: Build a comprehensive 20+ field extraction using a sample NIH R01 proposal from Dr. James Park. The document has budget breakdowns, key personnel, and specific aims to extract.
objectives: Add the sample NIH R01 proposal to your workspace
Create an Extraction with 15+ fields covering all document sections
Extract each budget category as its own field, plus personnel, aims, and compliance fields
tips: The NIH R01 has clearly structured sections: budget, key personnel, specific aims, vertebrate animals
Use the Allowed values setting on a field to constrain answers to a list (e.g., Human Subjects: Yes/No, Clinical Trial: Yes/No)
Mark fields like Co-Investigator as optional since there may be multiple

lessons.title: One-pass vs. two-pass extraction
lessons.objective: After this lesson, you'll know when to use two-pass vs. consensus extraction and what quality tradeoff you're making.
lessons.content:
An extraction strategy controls how the engine attempts the task. It does not establish that the returned values are true. Start with the source, field meanings and a small set of checked examples; then compare the available configurations against those examples.

One-pass mode uses a configured extraction pass for each document and field group. Two-pass mode first produces a draft, then attempts refinement. Each pass can use its own configured model and reasoning settings. Do not assume both passes use the same model, or that a mode label describes every setting in the saved extraction.

A second pass can help, but it can also retain or introduce an error. In the current engine, refinement failure can return the first-pass draft. A completed result therefore does not prove that two successful passes independently verified each value. Inspect the output and any available run information; source-check consequential values regardless of mode.

Field grouping, repetition, image handling and retries can affect the number of calls and resource use. Compare observed accuracy, unresolved values, time and usage on the same representative examples. Avoid promising a fixed cost ratio or choosing the most elaborate configuration without evidence.

**Practice:** Two configurations return the same budget. Both selected the annual amount when the task requires the total project amount. Explain why changing the number of passes alone does not resolve the field-definition error.

knowledgeCheck.question: Both extraction modes return the wrong annual budget. What should you check first?

options.text: Use more passes until the answers agree.
options.explanation: Agreement can preserve the same misunderstanding. Check the task and source before adding calls.

options.text: Clarify the requested budget scope, then rerun and compare the result with the source.
options.explanation: The field definition must identify the intended amount. A new result needs its own source check.

options.text: Accept the two-pass answer because refinement guarantees correctness.
options.explanation: Refinement can fail or repeat an error; the returned value still needs evidence.

lessons.title: Configuring fields for accuracy
lessons.objective: After this lesson, you'll be able to configure extraction fields that minimize hallucinations and missed values.
lessons.content:
A field needs a meaning that a reviewer can check. “Budget” could mean annual direct costs, total direct costs or total project costs including indirect costs. Name the intended amount, period and unit. “PI Name” distinguishes the investigator from a grants officer named elsewhere in the proposal.

Allowed values constrain a category to an authored set. They help control output shape; they do not prove that the selected label matches the source. A model can choose an allowed but incorrect value. Inspect the underlying statement as well as the returned label, and check behavior on the actual configured route.

Optionality describes whether the task permits a value to be absent. It is not a guarantee against invented answers. Conversely, a required field can still be missing or unsupported in the source. Keep that absence visible as a problem to resolve; do not force a plausible value merely to fill every cell. The structured extraction schema can represent null values, so a well-formed response can still be incomplete.

For a Yes/No question, missing evidence is not automatically No. Decide what counts as support for each category and how an absent statement will be represented. If the task permits an explicit unknown category, define its meaning. Otherwise preserve the unresolved value and explain the gap rather than silently changing the required categories.

### What chat creates and what you inspect in the editor

The current document-based creation tool reads the selected source and discovers candidate field names before its confirmation preview. It can create a reusable template from that discovered proposal. This route does not accept your full field-by-field Optional and Allowed values configuration as an authored schema. Asking for those settings in prose is not proof they were stored. Review the proposed source, name and fields, then inspect the saved template.

In the extraction editor, open the field’s settings to edit its meaning and inspect **Optional** and **Allowed values**. Use that supported route to correct an ambiguous field, set the permitted absence behavior and define category choices. Reopen or reread the saved field after editing to establish what will actually run. Do not increase the field count to compensate for a missing setting.

For example, define “Full project requested amount, USD, including indirect costs” rather than “Budget,” and check which source amount answers it. For an animal-use category, use only the task’s permitted categories and keep missing support unresolved. An Optional setting, an allowed category or a syntactically valid value does not establish source truth. Run the saved revision and compare the returned value with the relevant passage; preserve both the earlier result and the checked repair.

**Practice:** Rewrite “Animals” as a question about the assigned proposal’s vertebrate-animal use. Name the source statement that would establish Yes or No, and describe what you would record if neither is supported.

knowledgeCheck.question: A required compliance statement is absent. Which response preserves the evidence?

options.text: Return No because the document did not say Yes.
options.explanation: Absence of a statement does not necessarily establish the negative category.

options.text: Keep the value unresolved and identify the missing source support.
options.explanation: A required answer still needs evidence. Required does not authorize guessing.

options.text: Mark the field optional and assume any returned answer is safe.
options.explanation: Optionality concerns permitted absence; it does not validate the model’s answer.

lessons.title: Build a comprehensive extraction
lessons.content:
1. Create a new Extraction or expand an existing one to 15+ fields.
2. Group related fields logically — e.g., personnel fields together, budget fields together.
3. For any categorical field (status, type, category), open the field and fill in the **Allowed values** setting with the list of valid options.
4. Mark fields that may not always be present as optional.
5. Add descriptive titles to help the LLM understand ambiguous fields.
6. Run the extraction on a test document and review the results.
7. Iterate: adjust field names and add Allowed values for any fields that extracted poorly.

lessons.title: When to use consensus repetition
lessons.content:
Repetition compares multiple attempts at the same extraction. In the current engine, consensus starts with two attempts. If their normalized answers agree, it can return that result without a third attempt. A disagreement can trigger another attempt and field-level voting. Failure handling can also affect how many usable attempts remain.

This is not a promise of exactly three calls or a fixed three-times cost. Each attempt can itself use multiple passes and field groups. Inspect the effective configuration and observed usage when deciding whether the additional work is justified.

Agreement is a signal about consistency, not independent confirmation of the source. Repeated attempts can share the same ambiguous instruction, miss the same paragraph or choose the same unsupported value. A voted answer still needs comparison with the document. For a consequential amount or compliance category, identify the supporting passage and resolve any conflict before accepting it.

Start by fixing the source and field definition. Then compare repetition with a simpler configuration on representative examples, including missing information and conflicting amounts. Record which errors improved, which remained and what the extra work cost. Retain the option to leave a result unresolved rather than treating consensus as permission to release it.

**Practice:** Two attempts agree on a plausible date that appears nowhere in the assigned source. Decide what evidence would be needed before accepting it.

lessons.title: Worked example: fixing a weak field list
lessons.content:
Consider a practice case where “Budget” returns Year 1 direct costs, while the task requires the total for the full project including indirect costs. First inspect the source and establish what the returned amount actually represents. Do not treat a neat number or a matching currency symbol as proof of the requested meaning.

Repair the definition to state the period and included cost categories. If the source does not explicitly provide the required total, do not describe an inferred sum as an extracted quotation. Record that limitation and use a separately checked calculation only when the task permits it. Keep the original field revision and result so the reason for the change remains visible.

Save the revised extraction, inspect it, and run that revision on the same assigned source. Compare the new amount, unit and period with the source. Check the other required fields as well; a narrow repair does not establish that the rest of the output remains correct. Record remaining disagreements or missing values explicitly.

The useful evidence is the error you identified, the actual saved change, the linked new run and your source-based acceptance or further-repair decision. A setting change, an increased field count or a claim that quality improved is insufficient without that comparison. Do not invent a successful result for an illustrative repair.

**Practice:** A new field returns a different budget after your edit. Describe the check that distinguishes a genuine correction from merely a different answer.

lessons.title: Glossary & Review
lessons.content:
**Structured output:** A response constrained to an expected shape or set of categories. It can still contain null, incomplete or incorrect values. Validate meaning against the source after checking shape.

**Reasoning settings:** Model and pass configuration that can affect how an extraction is attempted. Effective behavior depends on the selected model and route. Do not treat a thinking label as an accuracy score or as evidence that a person reviewed the output.

**Field grouping:** The extraction engine can divide requested keys into groups when its chunking setting is enabled with a positive group size. It is not automatically triggered by every long field list, and it is different from splitting document text into retrieval chunks. Inspect the active setting and test interactions between related fields.

**Consensus:** Comparison and voting across repeated attempts. Agreement does not replace source support. Observe actual call and usage behavior instead of assuming a fixed number of attempts.

**Source reference:** A passage or location associated with a value. Check both that the passage belongs to the assigned source and that it supports the exact value and interpretation. The presence of a citation is not enough.

**Verified test case:** In the chat verification flow, proposing a test case runs an extraction and opens a guided verification session. The test case is created after the learner finalizes that review. Opening a session or an assistant saying “looks right” does not itself establish verified expected values or certification credit.

**Practice:** Explain the difference between an extraction result, a completed verification session and evidence that a certification outcome has been met.

subtitle: Chain Steps Together

objectives: Add the sample subaward agreement to your workspace
Build a 3-step workflow: Extraction + Prompt + Formatter
Verify the pipeline chains correctly from extraction to formatted report

Use the Prompt step to analyze obligations and flag key deadlines
